prize_parts.citation: for the invention and realisation of optical lattice clocks, reaching a fractional uncertainty of 10^-18 and opening a new regime of precision measurement

statement.case_for: I moved B061 from third in my opening ballot to my preferred configuration after reading the room, and I think the reasons are scientific and not only about support. The optical lattice clock is a measurement instrument in the strict sense: Katori's magic-wavelength idea lets many neutral atoms be interrogated without a lattice light shift, and Ye's group carried strontium to the 10^-18 systematic floor by controlling blackbody, lattice and collisional effects one at a time. That is the patient calibration and systematics work I respect most as an instrument builder. It is independently reproduced in Japan, the US, Germany, France and China, with direct clock-to-clock comparisons, so my usual question of whether it has been confirmed independently has a clear yes. The credit is compact (two names, a clear originator of the concept and a clear leader of the precision demonstration), and the outcomes are concrete: tests of constants and dark-matter couplings, relativistic geodesy at the centimetre scale, and the road to a new definition of the second. It also has the broadest opening support (five top-three placements and two first places), which matters to me as Chair, but I would not propose it on that basis alone.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that the 2005 prize to Hall and Hansch already honoured the frequency comb that makes optical clocks countable, and the 2012 prize to Wineland and Haroche covered quantum control of single systems and ion-clock work, so a committee could see this as an incremental follow-on. Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and others did essential work, and the field is still improving, with the SI second redefinition not yet decided. There is also a fair argument that B013 is the more original conceptual opening, and B009 the more significant new observational window; if the committee wants a discovery rather than a precision achievement, B061 is not the right choice.

responses.point: Danielsson ranks IceCube neutrino astronomy first as an instrument built to find exactly this, with a diffuse flux confirmed repeatedly and source evidence from TXS 0506+056 and NGC 1068.
responses.response: I agree with the science, and I ranked B009 first myself, so I will not pretend it is weak. But I have to be honest about where it stands in this committee: only three members rank it at all, Olsson places it sixth, and the credit problem is real. Halzen and Spiering are defensible instigators, yet AMANDA, Baikal and the IceCube founding group share the credit, and the individual source identifications are not yet confirmed by a second detector (KM3NeT and Baikal-GVD are not at that level). I would keep B009 as my second alternative and would support it in a later year, but I do not think I can chair a consensus around it now.

responses.point: Eriksson puts the Kane-Mele-Molenkamp topological insulators first as a conceptually clean, symmetry-protected classification, strongly confirmed and arguably overdue, while treating twisted bilayer graphene as slightly early.
responses.response: This is condensed matter, so I defer to you on the physics, and the confirmation record you describe is persuasive. My difficulty is attribution rather than merit: you note that Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang predicted the HgTe realisation and are not on the credited list, and Zhang has died. Add the 3D work of Fu, Kane, Mele and Moore-Balents and Hasan and the three-name limit makes a clean citation hard. It was also ranked by only three members, and the 2016 prize touched topological phases. I would like you to say whether the Kane-Mele and Molenkamp citation can stand without the BHZ prediction.

responses.point: Kroll ranks the optical lattice clock first, as a measurement instrument with fractional uncertainty near 10^-18, reproduced by several labs and enabling geodesy, constants tests and dark-matter searches.
responses.response: I broadly share this and have taken it as my preferred configuration. I would qualify one point: the lattice-clock story is not only Katori and Ye. Credit for the 10^-18 systematics also belongs to the JILA group members and to independent European and Chinese groups, so the citation should be worded for the invention and realisation of the lattice clock, not for the whole field of optical clocks. I would also push back mildly on treating the 2019 redefinition roadmap as a reason to act now; the definition is a metrology decision and should not drive a physics prize.

responses.point: Olsson ranks twisted bilayer graphene first: a prediction (Bistritzer-MacDonald) followed by the 2018 observation of correlated insulators and superconductivity, widely reproduced and a clean theory plus experiment trio.
responses.response: B013 is the strongest rival to my preferred choice and I ranked it second. The reproducibility is real, and the theory-plus-experiment attribution is cleaner than most. My reservation is maturity: Eriksson, Johansson and Mehlig all describe it as slightly early because the pairing mechanism is unresolved, and Yuan Cao, who was first author of the 2018 papers and a student at the time, is not among the credited names, which the committee should discuss openly. If the committee wants a discovery in quantum matter this year, I would support B013 without difficulty, so it is my first alternative.

responses.point: Johansson ranks circuit QED first as a very mature framework underlying superconducting qubits, with a natural continuity from the 2025 prize.
responses.response: I do not have the expertise to rank B018 and I will rely on you. My concern is the opposite of the usual one: the 2025 prize for macroscopic quantum tunnelling in circuits is recent, and awarding a closely related superconducting-circuit topic only a year later would look repetitive. The credited trio is also split between a lead experimenter and two theorists with different roles. I would want to hear from experts outside the committee about the relative weight of Schoelkopf's and Blais's contributions before that goes forward.

uncertainties: Whether the 2005 comb prize and the 2012 Wineland-Haroche prize make a lattice-clock prize look like a third award for precision laser spectroscopy.
Whether Katori and Ye are the right two names, given the contributions of Lemonde, Ludlow, Hinkley, Takamoto and others to the 10^-18 result.
Whether the committee prefers a precision-measurement achievement (B061) or a discovery in quantum matter (B013) this year; I have no strong view between them.
I am not an atomic or condensed-matter expert and rely on Kroll, Lindroth, Eriksson and Mehlig for the physics of B061, B013 and B019.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent for B061 or B013 from my profile. For disclosure: I am in the PAMELA, Fermi-LAT and XL-Calibur collaborations, and Fermi-LAT took part in multimessenger follow-up of IceCube alerts, so a mild field proximity to B009 is possible, and my cosmic-ray antimatter background is adjacent to B005, though I have no direct connection to the credited people.
